q: 301. Second phase B.O.D. is exerted because of the oxidation of ...........
options: carbonaceous matte into CO2 and H2O
explain: The first stage of BOD involves the oxidation of carbonaceous matter. The second stage, known as Nitrification or Nitrogenous BOD, occurs when specialized bacteria (Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) oxidize ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates.

q: 302. For any waste ...........
options: C.O.D. may be less than B.O.D.
C.O.D. is always greater than B.O.D.
depending upon the percentage of biodegradable matter, it may be either way
explain: Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) measures both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organic matter, whereas BOD only measures biodegradable matter. Therefore, COD is always greater than or equal to BOD.

q: 303. Result of C.O.D. is generally higher than that of B.O.D. because ...........
options: the strong oxidising conditions in the test
complete oxidation of organic and inorganic compounds
the stables compounds are being oxidized
explain: The COD test uses a strong chemical oxidizing agent (potassium dichromate in acidic medium), which can oxidize nearly all organic compounds, including those that are biologically resistant (stable), leading to higher oxygen demand values.

q: 304. In a C.O.D. test the most common interference is caused by the ions of ...........
explain: Chloride ions react with silver sulfate (the catalyst) and can be oxidized by dichromate, which leads to falsely high COD results. Mercuric sulfate is usually added to complex the chlorides and eliminate this interference.

q: 305. Time taken for C.O.D. test is about ...........
explain: While a standard BOD test takes 5 days, a COD test is much faster, typically requiring about 2 to 3 hours of refluxing (boiling) to complete the chemical oxidation.

q: 306. An advantage of C.O.D. test over B.O.D. test is ...........
options: it oxidized all matter including toxins
it cannot oxidize benzene, pyridine etc.
it is relatively a quick process
biodegradable matter cannot be distinguished from the rest
explain: The primary practical advantage of COD is the speed (3 hours vs 5 days), allowing for rapid monitoring and control of treatment plant processes.

q: 307. Presence of the following indicates recent pollution ...........
explain: Free ammonia or ammoniacal nitrogen is the first stage of nitrogen decomposition. Its presence indicates that the pollution occurred very recently and hasn't had time to oxidize into nitrites or nitrates.

q: 308. Presence of nitrogen in a waste water sample is due to the decomposition of ...........
explain: Proteins are complex organic compounds containing nitrogen. When proteins in sewage are decomposed by bacteria, they release nitrogen in various forms (ammonia, organic nitrogen).

q: 309. Eutrophication of a lake is ...........
options: enrichment of water quality with nutrients
deterioration of water bodies with biological growths
explain: Eutrophication is the process where a water body becomes overly enriched with nutrients (like phosphorus and nitrogen), leading to excessive growth of plants and algae.

q: 310. One of the important elements responsible for eutrophication is ...........
explain: Phosphates are often the 'limiting nutrient' in freshwater systems. Excess phosphorus from detergents or fertilizers is a primary driver of rapid algal blooms and eutrophication.

q: 311. Combined available chlorine means ...........
explain: Combined chlorine refers to chlorine that has reacted with ammonia in the water to form chloramines (Monochloramine and Dichloramine).

q: 312. Methemoglobinemia (Blue baby syndrome) is due to ...........
options: carbon monoxide replacing oxygen in hemoglobin
explain: High nitrate levels in drinking water are converted to nitrites in an infant's digestive system. These nitrites bind to hemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen, causing a bluish skin tint.

q: 313. Gastro intestinal irritation is produced because of excess of the following in water ...........
explain: Excessive concentrations of sulfates ($SO_4^{2-}$), especially when combined with magnesium (Epsom salt) or sodium (Glauber's salt), have a laxative effect and cause gastrointestinal distress.

q: 314. 'Dental caries' will be absent where the following is present ...........
explain: Mottled enamel (Fluorosis) occurs when there is an excess of fluoride. While aesthetically displeasing, teeth with fluorosis are highly resistant to dental caries (cavities).

q: 315. Concentration of fluorides desirable in water is ...........
explain: A small amount of fluoride (roughly 1 to 1.5 mg/l) is desirable to prevent tooth decay. Values exceeding 1.5-2.0 mg/l lead to mottling of teeth.

q: 316. More than 1 mg/l of fluorides ...........
options: prevent dental cavities and tooth decay in children
explain: Levels starting from 1 to 1.5 mg/l begin the threshold for fluorosis (mottling), though skeletal fluorosis usually requires much higher concentrations over long periods.

q: 317. Fluoridation is done to ...........
options: protect from both dental and skeletal fluorosis
explain: Fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to a public water supply to reduce tooth decay in the population, particularly children.

q: 318. Sudden increase in chloride concentration in water indicates ...........
options: ground water mixed with surface water
fresh water being mixed with sea water
explain: Human excreta and sewage contain high amounts of chlorides. A sudden spike in chloride levels in a previously low-chloride source is a strong indicator of sewage pollution.

q: 319. Kidney damage may be caused due to the excess concentration of ...........
explain: While chlorides are common, very high concentrations in drinking water are linked to physiological issues, including potential kidney stress, though chlorides are usually limited for taste (salinity) first.

q: 320. Absolutely soft waters are required for ...........
explain: Boilers require soft water to prevent the formation of hard scales (calcium/magnesium deposits) on heat-exchange surfaces, which reduce efficiency and can cause boiler explosions.

q: 321. Besides CA and Mg, the other metallic ions responsible for hardness are ...........
explain: While Calcium and Magnesium are the primary cause, multivalent metallic ions like Iron (Fe), Manganese (Mn), and Aluminum can also contribute to hardness.

q: 322. Hardness is desirable for ...........
options: wash water of sinks porcelain tubs
explain: Some epidemiological studies suggest that drinking moderately hard water is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular (heart) diseases compared to soft water.

q: 323. A desirable feature of hardness is ...........
options: scales formed inside pipes protect them from corrosion
explain: A thin layer of calcium carbonate scale (hardness) on the inner surface of metal pipes acts as a protective coating, preventing the pipe from corroding or leaching metals like lead into the water.

q: 324. Excess concentration of sodium salts in water causes ...........
explain: Sodium contributes to the total dissolved solids (TDS) and can impact the 'Pseudo-hardness' of water, though it doesn't cause true scale-forming hardness like Ca/Mg.

q: 325. Excess concentration of magnesium salts in water causes ...........
explain: Magnesium sulfate ($MgSO_4$) is known as Epsom salt and acts as a powerful laxative when consumed in high concentrations in drinking water.

q: 326. Iron in water causes ...........
explain: Iron and Manganese are notorious for causing reddish-brown or black stains on laundry, plumbing fixtures, and porcelain, even at very low concentrations (above 0.3 mg/l).

q: 327. Lead in water causes ...........
explain: Lead is a cumulative poison. It is highly toxic and causes damage to the central nervous system, kidneys, and reproductive system, especially in children.

q: 328. A communicable disease is ...........
explain: Communicable diseases are those that can be transmitted from one person to another. Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by bacteria (Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

q: 329. A water borne disease is ...........
explain: Water-borne diseases are caused by drinking contaminated water. Dysentery (amoebic or bacillary) is a classic example of a disease spread via the fecal-oral route through water.

q: 330. Due to improper storing of water the following disease spreads ...........
explain: Improper storage of water in open containers provides breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Filaria is transmitted by the Culex mosquito, which often breeds in stagnant, polluted water.

q: 331. For health, presence of traces of the following elements is a must in drinking water ...........
explain: Traces of fluoride (around 1 mg/l) prevent dental caries, and iodine is essential for the proper functioning of the thyroid gland to prevent goitre.

q: 332. A water borne virus infection is ...........
explain: Infectious Hepatitis (Jaundice) is caused by the Hepatitis A or E virus, which is commonly transmitted through contaminated water supplies.

q: 333. An indicator organism is ...........
options: non-pathogenic bacteria of the same family of pathogens
explain: An indicator organism (like E. coli) is a non-pathogenic bacterium that lives in the same environment as pathogens. Its presence indicates that the water is contaminated and pathogens might also be present.

q: 334. An indicator organism ...........
options: is of human origin but not found in water
harmless bacterium found in some types of waters
should produce more gas when incubated
explain: The key requirement for a good indicator is that it must be present whenever pathogens are present, meaning it must originate from the same source (human/animal intestines).

q: 335. Bacteria utilize ...........
explain: Bacteria can only transport nutrients across their cell membranes if the food is in a dissolved, soluble form. They often secrete enzymes to break down solids into soluble molecules first.

q: 336. Autotrophic bacteria derive energy from ...........
explain: Autotrophic bacteria use inorganic substances (like CO2, ammonia, or sulfur) as their carbon and energy source, whereas heterotrophs require organic matter.

q: 337. Oily odour and taste producing substances are produced by ...........
explain: Certain types of algae (like Diatoms or Synura) release oils and decomposition products that impart distinct fishy, oily, or grassy tastes and odors to water.

q: 338. An indicator organism for bacteriological quality of water is ...........
explain: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is the standard indicator organism because it is present in massive numbers in the intestines of warm-blooded animals and is easy to detect.

q: 339. In drinking water number of coliform bacteria should not exceed ...........
explain: For treated drinking water, the standard limit is strict: there should be zero coliforms per 100 ml of sample to ensure safety from pathogens.

q: 340. A factor affecting domestic demand is ...........
options: dead end system or reticulation system of network of pipes
water supplied is soft or hard
explain: Climate significantly affects domestic use; water consumption is much higher in hot, dry climates for bathing, gardening, and cooling compared to cold regions.

q: 341. For an old city with constraints for growth the best method of forecasting future population is ...........
explain: The Arithmetical Increase Method assumes a constant rate of growth and is most suitable for old, large cities that have reached their saturation point and have limited room for expansion.

q: 342. If the present population of a city is 'a', rate of increase per decade is 'b', incremental increase per decade is 'c', percentage growth per decade is 'r', then population after 'n' decades by incremental increase method is ...........
explain: The incremental increase method combines the arithmetic increase ('b' per decade) with the average of the net increments ('c'). The formula is Pn = P + n.X + [n(n+1)/2].Y.

q: 343. Design period mainly depends on ...........
options: percentage interest at which the loan is taken
capacity of the municipality to repay
explain: The design period (how long the project should last) is chosen based on how fast the population is growing. Rapid growth requires shorter design periods to avoid obsolescence.

q: 344. Ground water is ...........
options: free from suspended solids but contain dissolved solids
free from harmful bacteria but may have suspended solids
free from floating impurities but may have suspended solids
free from dissolved solids but may have colloidal solids
explain: As water percolates through soil layers, it is naturally filtered, removing suspended particles. However, it dissolves minerals from the rocks, leading to high dissolved solid content.

q: 345. A shadow well is one tapping an aquifer ...........
options: sandwiched in between two impervious layers
runs through a number of strata
explain: A shallow well (often called an unconfined or phreatic well) taps the uppermost water table which is not under pressure and is nearest to the ground surface.

options: easy gets dried up during summer
is not deeper than a shallow well
is formed by just tapping the nearest aquifer to the ground
explain: Deep wells tap confined aquifers below impervious layers. These sources are more reliable and provide a more constant discharge compared to shallow wells which fluctuate with rainfall.

q: 347. A river intake may be situated on ...........
options: the convex side of a curved course
explain: A straight reach of the river is preferred for intakes to avoid the erosion found on concave banks and the silting/deposition found on convex banks.

q: 348. River water may have ...........
options: more suspended solids and less dissolved solids
more dissolved solids and less suspended solids
more dissolved solids and less floating solids
explain: Surface waters like rivers are exposed to runoff, which brings in high amounts of suspended silt and clay, but they generally have lower contact time with minerals compared to groundwater.

q: 349. A good source of water requiring practically the least treatment is ...........
explain: Elevated lakes in mountainous regions are often far from human pollution and have natural sedimentation, making the water very pure and sometimes requiring only disinfection.

q: 350. Sedimentation may not be required for water from a ...........
explain: Water from deep wells has already undergone extensive natural filtration through soil and rock layers, so it contains almost no suspended solids that would require sedimentation.

q: 351. Waters from the following source is likely to be hard ...........
explain: Groundwater, especially from deep wells, has a longer contact time with underground mineral-bearing rocks (like limestone), causing more calcium and magnesium to dissolve into the water.

q: 352. Permissible velocity through coarse screens is not greater than ...........
explain: The velocity through the openings of a coarse screen (rack) is typically kept around 0.75 to 1 m/s. Higher velocities might force debris through the bars, while lower velocities cause excessive head loss.

q: 353. A discrete particle is one ...........
options: whose settling is unaffected by the neighbouring particles
whose settling influence neighbouring particles, i.e., due to mass action
for which hindered settling takes place
explain: Discrete particles (Type-1 settling) do not change their size, shape, or weight during settling. In dilute suspensions, they settle individually without interacting with other particles.

q: 354. Generally 'flow through period' of a sedimentation tank is ...........
options: exactly equal to the detention period
sometime more and some time less
explain: The theoretical detention period (V/Q) assumes ideal flow. In reality, short-circuiting and dead zones cause the actual 'flow through period' to be less than the theoretical detention time.

q: 355. Over flow rate of a sedimentation tank is ...........
explain: The Surface Overflow Rate (SOR) is defined as the volume of water applied per unit time per unit of horizontal (plan) surface area. It determines the settling efficiency of the tank.

q: 356. Coagulant should be used for sedimentation when turbidity of raw water exceeds ...........
explain: Plain sedimentation is effective only for coarse particles. When turbidity exceeds 50 NTU/units, chemical coagulants are needed to aggregate fine colloidal particles into settleable flocs.

q: 357. Coagulant is affected because of higher concentration of ...........
explain: Coagulants like Alum require alkalinity (usually in the form of bicarbonates) to react and form the gelatinous precipitate (floc). If alkalinity is too low or imbalanced, the process is less effective.

q: 358. Coagulating power of a chemical increases with its ...........
explain: According to the Schulze-Hardy rule, the coagulating power of an electrolyte increases rapidly with the valency of the ion. For example, $Al^{3+}$ is much more effective than $Na^+$.

q: 359. Colloidal particles are associated with ...........
explain: Colloidal particles are so small that they are kept in suspension by 'Brownian movement'—the random bombardment by water molecules—preventing them from settling by gravity alone.

q: 360. Lime is added to water or waste samples to ...........
options: destabilize colloidal oil and organic emulsion suspension
to assist precipitation of hydroxides of metals by lowering their pH
convert calcium carbonate to calcium bicarbonate
explain: Lime (Calcium Hydroxide) is often used to adjust pH and provide the necessary conditions to destabilize emulsions and assist in the precipitation of organic matter.

q: 361. Optimum dose of coagulant means the least dose that produces ...........
options: floc whose density is very high
explain: The 'Optimum Dose' (determined by a Jar Test) is the minimum amount of chemical required to form a heavy, large, and tough floc that settles quickly, leaving the water clear.

q: 362. Methamoglobinemia is due to ...........
explain: High concentrations of nitrates in water cause 'Blue Baby' syndrome. Note: The nitrates are reduced to nitrites in the body, but the original pollutant in the water supply is measured as nitrates.

q: 363. When alumina is used as a coagulant for neutral water the end products obtained are ...........
explain: Alum reacts with calcium bicarbonate alkalinity to form Aluminum Hydroxide (the floc), Calcium Sulfate (permanent hardness), and Carbon Dioxide (which increases acidity).

q: 364. A coagulant aid is one which ...........
explain: Coagulant aids (like activated silica or polyelectrolytes) are added to produce larger, heavier, and tougher flocs, especially when the water is very cold or very low in turbidity.

q: 365. Copperas is ...........
explain: Copperas is the common name for Ferrous Sulfate ($FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O$). It is used as a coagulant, typically in conjunction with lime.

q: 366. Chlorinated copperas is ...........
explain: When chlorine is added to a solution of copperas (ferrous sulfate), it oxidizes it to form a mixture of Ferric Sulfate and Ferric Chloride, which is a very effective coagulant.

q: 367. Detention time in a 'flocculator' is ...........
explain: After flash mixing, water is slowly agitated in a flocculator for 20-30 minutes to allow the small particles to collide and grow into larger flocs.

q: 368. Detention time in a flash mixer is ...........
explain: Flash mixing is a very rapid process intended to disperse the coagulant uniformly throughout the water, typically taking less than a minute.

q: 369. Schmutzdecke will be formed in ...........
options: both slow sand and pressure filters
explain: Schmutzdecke (dirty skin) is a biological layer of algae, bacteria, and protozoa that forms on the surface of a Slow Sand Filter and is responsible for its high efficiency.

q: 370. Back washing is highly effective in case of ...........
explain: Rapid sand and pressure filters are cleaned by reversing the flow of water (backwashing) to agitate the bed and remove trapped impurities. Slow sand filters are cleaned by scraping the top layer.

q: 371. Fine sand is used as media in case of ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Slow sand filters use a finer grade of sand ($D_{10}$ approx. 0.2 to 0.3 mm) to ensure effective filtration at very low flow rates.

q: 372. Effluent from this unit requires no other treatment other than disinfection ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Slow sand filters are so efficient at removing bacteria (98-99%) and turbidity that the treated water is generally safe enough to require only minimal chlorination.

q: 373. Coagulant may not be added for treatment before ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Slow sand filters are designed to treat relatively clear water. Adding coagulants would quickly clog the fine sand and destroy the Schmutzdecke layer.

q: 374. Iso-electric point is the pH value at which ...........
options: the electrical charge of a colloid is zero
the colloidal charge of a particle is zero
ideal concentration of coagulant is present for rapid coagulation
explain: The Iso-electric point is the specific pH where the net surface charge (Zeta potential) of the particles becomes zero, allowing them to aggregate easily.

q: 375. Coagulant is a must before letting water into ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Rapid sand filters use coarser sand and higher rates of filtration; they rely entirely on the prior formation of chemical flocs to trap impurities.

q: 376. A highly flexible filter is ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Rapid sand filters are flexible because their filtration rate can be adjusted, they handle varying turbidity well, and they require much less space than slow sand filters.

q: 377. This is used to treat swimming pool water ...........
options: both rapid and slow sand filters
explain: Pressure filters are compact and can be easily integrated into the closed-loop pumping systems used for swimming pools.

q: 378. Disinfection is the process of ...........
options: removal of causative organic for disease
explain: Disinfection specifically targets 'pathogens' (disease-causing organisms). It does not necessarily kill all bacteria or spores (that would be sterilization).

q: 379. One of the physical agents responsible for disinfection is ...........
explain: UV radiation is a physical process that disrupts the DNA of microorganisms, preventing them from reproducing. Ozone, Lime, and Heat are chemical or thermal agents.

q: 380. A desirable property of a disinfectant is that it should ...........
options: not alter the quality of water
explain: An ideal disinfectant should kill pathogens effectively without changing the taste, odor, or chemical safety of the water for the consumer.

q: 381. Efficiency of disinfection is ...........
explain: Based on Chick's Law, the rate of kill is proportional to the number of organisms remaining: $log_{10}(N_0/N_t) = kt$, where $N_0$ is the initial count and $N_t$ is the count at time $t$.

q: 382. Mud balls are formed in a filter because of ...........
options: raw water rolling over the filter surface
bond developed between impurities and sand grains due to inefficient back washing
explain: If backwashing is insufficient, sticky organic matter and silt accumulate on sand grains, forming clumps or 'mud balls' that sink and clog the filter bed.

q: 383. Sterilization is ...........
explain: Sterilization is a total process that destroys all forms of microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial spores.

q: 384. A heavy metal capable of disinfecting is ...........
explain: Silver has oligodynamic properties, meaning tiny amounts can kill bacteria. It is sometimes used for small-scale or specialized disinfection.

q: 385. To disinfect swimming pool water, we use ...........
explain: While chlorine is common, Bromine is often preferred for swimming pools (especially indoor ones) because it is more stable in warm water and produces less irritating odors (bromamines).

q: 386. Iodine is used to disinfect ...........
options: raw water without any other treatment
explain: Iodine is effective and portable, making it suitable for field use, travelers, or small emergency water supplies, though it is not used for large municipal systems.

q: 387. The only disinfectant available in the three states (solid, liquid and gas) is ...........
explain: Chlorine is available as a gas ($Cl_2$), a liquid (Sodium Hypochlorite), and a solid (Bleaching powder/Calcium Hypochlorite).

q: 388. Pick up a disinfectant from the following ...........
explain: Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$) is a powerful oxidizing agent used to remove iron, manganese, and to disinfect well water supplies.

q: 389. Residual chlorine is given out when ...........
options: chlorine required for disinfection and oxidation of organic matter is less than applied chlorine
chlorine required is more than that supplied
chlorine applied is just sufficient to that required
explain: Residual Chlorine = Applied Chlorine - Chlorine Demand. It is the amount left over to provide continued protection against re-contamination.

q: 390. In chlorination the most effective kill is due to ...........
explain: Hypochlorous acid ($HOCl$) is about 80 times more effective at killing microorganisms than the Hypochlorite ion ($OCl^-$).

q: 391. Disinfection ability of a chemical depends on ...........
options: concentration of disinfectant x time of concentration
explain: This is known as the 'Ct' concept (Concentration x Time). A lower concentration requires a longer contact time to achieve the same level of disinfection.

q: 392. The usual amount of residual chlorine required after 10 minutes of contact is ...........
explain: Public health standards generally require a minimum free residual of 0.2 mg/l to ensure the water remains safe as it travels through the distribution network.

q: 393. 'Free chlorine residual' means ...........
explain: Free chlorine residual specifically refers to the sum of Hypochlorous acid and Hypochlorite ions available in the water.

q: 394. 'Pre-chlorination' is done to ...........
explain: Pre-chlorination (adding chlorine before filtration) helps control algae growth in basins, oxidizes iron/manganese, and reduces tastes and odors caused by organic matter.

q: 395. Plain chlorination is done after ...........
explain: Plain chlorination refers to disinfecting water that is otherwise clean (like clear lake or groundwater) and only requires sedimentation before the final chlorine dose.

q: 396. Super chlorination is done ...........
options: when no other treatment is resorted to
explain: Super chlorination involves applying a very high dose of chlorine (e.g., 5-15 mg/l) during emergencies like disease outbreaks to ensure total destruction of pathogens.

q: 397. Dechlorination is done with ...........
explain: After super-chlorination, excess chlorine must be removed so the water is drinkable. Sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) or Sodium Thiosulfate are common dechlorinating agents.

q: 398. A main disadvantage of chlorine as disinfectant is ...........
explain: Chlorine is a strong oxidizing agent and, in the presence of moisture, is highly corrosive to metal pipes and equipment.

q: 399. Presence of (residual) chlorine is readily detected by ...........
explain: The Orthotolidine test (OT test) is the standard method for determining residual chlorine; the sample turns yellow in the presence of chlorine.

q: 400. Besides disinfection chlorination is effective in the removal of ...........
explain: Chlorine oxidizes organic coloring matter and iron/manganese compounds, effectively bleaching and reducing the color of the water.
